paragraphs.heading: What spiral arms are
paragraphs.text: Spiral arms are a defining feature of spiral galaxies. They are spiral-shaped regions within a galaxy's disc that shine brighter than the space around them. Most spiral galaxies have two or more arms, and together they make up the galaxy's spiral pattern. In galaxies without a bar the arms usually start near the center, while in barred galaxies they begin at the ends of the bar.

paragraphs.heading: What is in them
paragraphs.text: Arms are more than bright streaks. Compared with the rest of the disc, they hold more interstellar gas and dust, more bright stars and star clusters, and more bursts of star formation, and they look bluer and carry stronger magnetic fields. In some galaxies the arms supply 40 to 50% of all the light. They are best known for their young stars, yet old stars are also more concentrated in them.

paragraphs.heading: Different light, different look
paragraphs.text: How the arms look depends on the kind of light used. In blue and ultraviolet light they stand out sharply, thanks to blue supergiant stars. In red and near-infrared light older stars add more, so the arms look smoother but less contrasted. Glowing dust makes them bright in the far infrared, and neutral hydrogen and molecules make them bright in radio.

paragraphs.heading: Many kinds of arms
paragraphs.text: Galaxies differ a lot in how their arms look. Grand design spirals, about 10% of spirals, show two clear, symmetrical arms running across the whole galaxy. Flocculent spirals, about 30%, have many short pieces of arm that do not join up. The rest are called multi-armed and mix features of both. In Hubble's classification, Sa and SBa galaxies have tight, smooth arms, while Sc and SBc galaxies have loose, knotty ones.

paragraphs.heading: Arms and the whole galaxy
paragraphs.text: The arms are linked to other traits of their galaxy. How tightly they twist is related to the mass of the supermassive black hole at the center, and to how much of the galaxy's light comes from its bulge.

paragraphs.heading: A long-lived pattern
paragraphs.text: Lord Rosse first spotted spiral structure in 1850, in the galaxy M51. Spirals are common: about two thirds of massive galaxies are spiral galaxies. Arms have been seen in galaxies at redshifts up to about z ≈ 1, which means as they were when the universe was less than half its present age, and this suggests spiral structure lasts a long time. Two main theories explain where arms come from: density wave theory, and a model of stochastic self-propagating star formation. They describe different kinds of spiral structure rather than ruling each other out.
